title: Admin password card: questions before anything is drawn

steps.path: The card that appears when the assistant wants to run an admin (sudo) command
steps.headline: Where should you type your admin password when the assistant needs it?
steps.today: When the assistant wants an admin command, a card asks you to approve it. If you approve, the command fails, because it has no way to ask you for your password.
steps.problem: Anything that needs admin rights (installing system software, drivers, changing system settings) can't be done from chat. The assistant gives up or hands you a command to paste into a terminal.
steps.proposal: After you approve, you type your password and the command runs. The question is whose box you type it into.

options.label: In the chat card
pros: Looks like the rest of the app and sits right next to the command it unlocks.
Works on every Mac and Linux computer the same way.
Can show exactly which command wants admin rights, and say when the password was wrong.
cons: The app handles your password for a moment, so we must build the safety carefully (the next pages cover that).

options.label: Computer's own window
options.summary: The same pop-up your computer uses for system updates.
pros: The app never touches your password at all.
cons: Missing on some Linux setups, so there it would still fail.
Doesn't say which command is asking, so you approve something you can't see.
Looks different on every computer; easy to confuse with a fake pop-up.

steps.path: The card that appears when the assistant wants to run an admin command
steps.headline: Should approving and typing the password happen on one card, or two in a row?
steps.today: Admin commands already show an approval card with the command on it (in Full auto, it's the 'Stopped before an admin command' band).
steps.problem: Adding a separate password step after approval means two stops for one decision.
steps.proposal: Pick how the two steps fit together.

options.label: One card
options.summary: The command, a password box and Run / Skip, all together. Typing the password and pressing Run is the approval.
pros: You never approve a command and then find a second surprise waiting.
cons: The approval card gets a bit taller for admin commands.

options.label: Approve, then password
pros: The approval card stays exactly as it looks today.
cons: If you walk away after approving, the command sits waiting on a password card you may not notice.

steps.headline: When a command asks for admin rights partway through, should the password card appear then?
steps.today: Some commands don't start with 'sudo' but ask for admin rights partway through, like an install script. Those get no admin card at all, and quietly fail at the admin step.
steps.problem: Installers are exactly the commands you'd want to run from chat, and they're the ones that fail silently.
steps.proposal: The moment any command asks for admin rights, the password card appears naming the exact step that wants it (for example 'install.sh wants to run: pacman -S rocm'). Nothing gets admin rights without that card.

options.label: Show the card
pros: You see the exact admin step, not just the outer command's name, so it's more honest than today's card.
cons: A card can appear while a command is already running, which is new.
A script with several admin steps may ask several times (see next page).

options.label: Let it fail
options.summary: Only commands that visibly start with sudo get the card.
pros: Cards only ever appear before a command starts.
cons: Installers keep failing silently from chat.

steps.headline: Should this card handle only your computer's admin password, or other passwords too?
steps.today: No command the assistant runs can ask you for any password: admin, GitHub login, SSH key or database.
steps.problem: Each kind of password goes somewhere different (your computer, a website, a server), so each has its own risks.
steps.proposal: Pick what the first version covers.

options.label: Admin password only
pros: One clear job: 'your computer's password, to run this as admin'.
Smallest thing to get right and check for holes.
cons: A command that wants a website or SSH password still fails, as today.

options.label: Any password prompt
pros: Every command that asks for a password works from chat.
cons: The app can't reliably tell who's asking, so a command could trick you into typing a password for something else.
Much more to build and to check for holes.

steps.intro: These decide how much one password unlocks, and where you can type it from.

steps.path: After you have typed your admin password once
steps.headline: After your password works once, should the next admin step ask again?
steps.today: In a terminal, after you type your admin password, your computer remembers it for 5 to 15 minutes and later admin commands run without asking.
steps.problem: If the app let that memory stand, one password could quietly unlock the assistant's later admin commands, which you never saw.
steps.proposal: Pick how much one password unlocks.

options.label: Ask every time
options.summary: After each command finishes, the app tells your computer to forget. Every admin step shows the card.
pros: One password unlocks exactly one thing you saw.
Nothing lingers after you walk away.
cons: An installer with three admin steps asks three times.
If you also use sudo in your own terminal, it will ask you for the password again there too (your computer can only forget everything at once).

options.label: Once per command
options.summary: Within one command the computer's normal memory applies; the next command asks again.
pros: An installer asks once, not three times.
Your own terminal is left alone.
cons: The second and third admin steps inside that one command run without showing you what they are.

steps.path: A phone or browser paired to your computer
steps.headline: Should you be able to type your admin password from your paired phone or browser?
steps.today: Approval cards show on your paired phone and browser too, and you can answer them from there.
steps.problem: Your password would travel across your private network to reach the computer. That link is encrypted, but it's one more place the password passes through.
steps.proposal: Pick where the password card works.

options.label: This computer only
pros: Your password only ever exists on the computer it unlocks.
cons: Away from the computer, the phone shows 'Type your password on your computer' and the command waits.

options.label: Phone and browser too
pros: You can unblock an install from your couch.
cons: The password crosses your network, and someone holding your unlocked phone could type it.

steps.path: After an admin command has started
steps.headline: If an admin command starts something that keeps running, should the app show it's still running as admin?
steps.today: Some admin commands start a program that stays running after the command ends, such as a server. Nothing marks that it still has full control of your computer.
steps.problem: One approval could quietly give something admin power for hours.
steps.proposal: Yes: a small 'still running as admin' marker with a Stop button until it ends. No: leave it for later; this first version covers the password card only. Don't know: I'll leave it out and note it as a follow-up.

steps.intro: These aren't questions. They're the rules I'll build to. Mark any you disagree with.

steps.headline: Your password is never saved, never shown to the assistant, and never written into chat history.
steps.changed: The password goes straight from the box to your computer's admin program, then is erased from memory. The assistant and chat history only ever see 'admin password given'.
steps.notice: You type it every time. There's no 'Always allow' and no 'remember my password'.

steps.headline: The card's wording is always the app's own, never text supplied by the command.
steps.changed: A command can choose its own password message (for example 'Enter your Google password'). The card ignores that and always says it's your computer password, for the command shown.
steps.notice: A misbehaving command can't use the card to trick you into typing a different password.

steps.headline: The password is only ever handed to your computer's real admin program, never to anything pretending to be it.
steps.changed: Before sending the password, the app checks that the thing asking for it is your computer's genuine admin program. A fake one the assistant made earlier gets nothing.
steps.notice: Nothing, unless something fake asks. Then the card doesn't appear and the command fails.
steps.risk: Honest limit: if something harmful is already running on your computer as you, it could still watch the password pass by. The same is true when you type sudo in a terminal.

steps.headline: Full auto still stops for every admin password, and helpers' admin requests come to you.
steps.changed: Unchanged from today: Full auto stops before admin commands. A helper's admin request shows on your card, labelled with the helper's name.
steps.notice: No mode or helper can run an admin command without you typing the password.

steps.headline: A wrong password says so and lets you try again, with a warning before your computer locks you out.
steps.changed: Your computer allows 3 tries. After a wrong one the card says 'Wrong password, 2 tries left'. Some Linux computers lock sudo for about 10 minutes after 3 wrong tries, and the card warns you before the last one.
steps.notice: A typo costs one retry, not a failed command.

steps.headline: The card waits for you with no time limit; Skip stops the command.
steps.changed: Like every other approval card, it waits until you answer. Skip, or closing the session, stops the command safely.
steps.notice: You can step away and answer later.

steps.headline: This is for Mac and Linux. Windows and phones are left unchanged.
steps.changed: Windows has no admin password step to type in: it uses its own Yes/No pop-up. Phones can't run admin commands at all.
steps.notice: On Windows, admin commands behave exactly as today.
